extracted.intended_audience: AI researchers, cognitive scientists, and mathematicians interested in problem-solving methods and heuristics
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of Polya-style auxiliary-problem methods and their relation to AI problem-space paradigms, focusing on how auxiliary problems are found, represented, and used. Discusses limits of object-centered problem spaces and introduces notions such as wild/tame subproblems and the connection problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem space definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem space consists of a set of states and a set of operators that when applied to states yield new states; a problem is given by an initial state and a class of goal states plus possibly path constraints (the task is to get from the initial state to a goal state along a permissible path).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the basic formal apparatus for casting tasks in AI: clearly identify states, operators, initial state, goal states, and path constraints. The formulation implies that problem solving is search in this space; evaluation of methods should check how they define and manipulate these components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic search characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic search: combinatorial search modulated by whatever knowledge (heuristics) can be brought to bear; uncertainty in operator application translates into search complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess methods by the nature/amount of domain knowledge they use (general vs specific), how they select/reject operators/states, evaluation functions, and how much combinatorial search remains. Anti-pattern: treating all search as blind without leveraging heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-solver competence as union of problem spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem solver's basic capabilities are expressed by the problem spaces it can employ; its total competence is the union of those spaces (problems outside those spaces lie outside its competence or comprehension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a system, consider which problem spaces it supports and whether those spaces cover the intended class of problems; competence is measured by coverage and ability to bring heuristics to bear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-centered problem space
rubrics_metrics.description: Object-centered problem space: states are generated from the objects in the problem by structural composition operations (e.g., expressions, diagrams, data structures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights a prevalent AI paradigm (geometry expressions, algebraic expressions, circuit analyses). Limitation: such spaces represent objects/expressions rather than problems, making it hard to represent or transform auxiliary problems as independent problems (loses ability to start with an imperfect/wrong proof and transform it into a good one).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-centered problem space
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem-centered problem space: states are generated from problem statements (including constraints and conditions) rather than by decomposing objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested as the alternative needed to represent many auxiliary problems; evaluate systems on whether their states encode problem statements/constraints so that auxiliary problems can be represented and manipulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya's Auxiliary-Problem Method (three steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary-problem method: (1) find an auxiliary problem, (2) solve the auxiliary problem, (3) use the auxiliary problem (result, method, or attempt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or designing problem-solving approaches, verify support for each stage and for their independence — especially that the 'use' step is handled (not just the solving step). Many AI methods focus on the middle recursive step but neglect finding and using.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya suggestion 1: Have you seen the problem before?
rubrics_metrics.description: Find auxiliary problems by recognizing identical prior problems from experience/memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes retrieval-based generation: evaluate whether the system can recall exact past problems as potential auxiliaries. Note: this is non-constructive (memory retrieval) rather than generative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya suggestion 2: Have you seen the problem in a different form?
rubrics_metrics.description: Find auxiliary problems by recognizing the same problem presented differently (a different formulation or representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess capacity for representation mapping or canonicalization to detect equivalent problems across forms. This is retrieval/recognition-heavy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya suggestion 3: Do you know a familiar problem with the same unknown?
rubrics_metrics.description: Find auxiliary problems by recalling problems that ask for the same unknown quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a system can index problems by unknowns/goals to retrieve useful analogs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya suggestion 4: Do you know a familiar problem with a similar unknown?
rubrics_metrics.description: Find auxiliary problems by recalling problems with closely related (but not identical) unknowns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests analogical retrieval and ability to adapt similar-goal solutions to the current problem; again often retrieval-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya suggestion 5: Here is a related problem solved before; could you use its result or methods?
rubrics_metrics.description: Use previously solved related problems: their results, their methods, or both as auxiliaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a system can identify and exploit transfer from previously solved problems (method transfer or result reuse). This is akin to oracle-provided auxiliaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya suggestion 6: Solve first some related problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate an auxiliary by creating and solving a related but simpler/more tractable problem before returning to the main problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires ability to propose related problems and then treat their solutions as subgoals — a mix of generative and recursive capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya suggestion 7: Do you know a more accessible related general problem?
rubrics_metrics.description: Find an auxiliary by replacing the original with a more general but easier-to-handle problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess systems for capability to generalize and then instantiate; generative operators like AM's generalize/specialize are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya suggestion 8: Do you know a more special problem?
rubrics_metrics.description: Find an auxiliary by specializing the problem (consider special cases) to make it solvable or informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization is commonly usable in AI (e.g., specialize to c=0 yielding triangle in trapezoid example); systems should support systematic specialization as a generator of auxiliaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya suggestion 9: Do you know an analogous problem?
rubrics_metrics.description: Recall an analogous problem in a different domain or context that may provide useful parallels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates analogical reasoning abilities; retrieval from cross-domain memory and mapping of structure are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya suggestion 10: Use the data somehow (create a problem using the same data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate an auxiliary by reframing or reusing the given data to pose a new problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests creativity in data reinterpretation — e.g., forming geometric constructions from numeric data — and the ability to judge usefulness of the new posed problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya suggestion 11: Solve the problem keeping only part of the condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an auxiliary by dropping some conditions or constraints (simplify constraints) and solve the resulting problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is specific and constructive; AI planning methods sometimes emulate it (e.g., dropping a condition). Evaluate whether the system can systematically relax constraints and reason about implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya suggestion 12: Restate the problem (restate it still differently)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate auxiliaries by reformulating or restating the problem multiple ways to reveal different approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess linguistic/representational flexibility: paraphrasing, reframing, and alternative formalizations. Often the last two suggestions (drop condition, restate) are most amenable to current AI techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation mode: retrieval/oracle vs generative operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary problems may be retrieved from long-term memory or supplied by an oracle (non-constructive), whereas typical AI subproblems are generated constructively by operators (generative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing systems, distinguish whether auxiliaries come from recall/analogy/oracle or from generative operators (means-ends style). Retrieval-driven auxiliaries may not form searchable spaces; generative ones can be embedded in a search architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya's taxonomy for using an auxiliary problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Three ways to use a solved auxiliary problem: (1) use the result, (2) use the method, (3) use the attempt (the failed attempt suggesting new auxiliaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate systems on each of these use-modes. 'Use the attempt' is often salvage-based and arises after failures; systems should support both direct transfer and inspection of unsuccessful attempts for new leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wild vs Tame subproblems
rubrics_metrics.description: Wild subproblem: a subproblem whose use in the main problem remains a problem even after it is solved. Tame subproblem: how to use it is already known when it is generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is crucial: AI methods typically produce tame subproblems (predictable use). Evaluate whether a system can handle wild subproblems (i.e., can solve the connection problem). Wild subproblems require additional mechanisms to connect solutions back to the main problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: The connection problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Connection problem: the subproblem of how to connect a solved auxiliary problem with the main problem — i.e., how a solved auxiliary can be used to make progress on the main problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'using' an auxiliary as a separate problem-solving task. Systems should be evaluated on their ability to pose and solve connection problems (examples: reducing main problem to special case, constructing embeddings or transforms).

rubrics_metrics.name: AI subproblem design: coordinated result-use (means-ends and AND/OR trees)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many AI methods the operators that create subproblems also specify exactly what to do with their results (e.g., means-ends analysis reduces difference producing a new state from which to continue; SAINT's method for integrals explicitly replaces integrals with results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging algorithmic approaches, check whether subproblem generation and result-application are coordinated. This predictable coordination creates 'tame' subproblems and is an advantage in controllable automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic mechanisms for bringing knowledge to bear
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms include selection and rejection of operators and states, evaluation functions, models, causality analysis, planning, macro-objects, dependency-directed backtracking, creation of plan hierarchies, and other ways to operationalize heuristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate which mechanisms a system uses to apply heuristic knowledge and how effectively they reduce combinatorial search. Example anti-patterns: lacking causality analysis (leads to blind backtracking) or lacking plan hierarchies (leads to poor coordination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary problems as isolated points vs elements of a space
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary problems may not form a coherent problem space but instead be isolated problems with weak relations to the main problem (retrieved from memory or oracle) rather than being generatively composed in a searchable space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether auxiliaries are generated within a searchable space (enabling planning and evaluation) or are isolated recollections; different system architectures are needed for each case. AI architectures assuming a space may fail to handle isolated, retrieval-based auxiliaries.
